test-strategy.md:
## Why it exists

A test is a program that fails when your other program stops doing what you meant. Its value is not "proving correctness" (testing cannot prove the absence of bugs) but **buying the freedom to change code without fear**. Teams with a fast, trustworthy test suite refactor, upgrade dependencies and ship on Fridays; teams without one freeze their code, because every change might break something nobody remembers.

**Mental model:** think of tests as a portfolio with a budget of speed and trust. Cheap, fast tests (unit) tell you quickly that a rule is broken. Expensive, slow tests (end to end) tell you that the whole thing hangs together. A healthy suite has many of the first, enough of the second to cover the critical journeys, and a few in between that check the seams where components meet, because that is where most real bugs live.

## How it works

### The kinds of tests

- **Unit tests** exercise one function or class in isolation, run in milliseconds, and need no network or database. Best for rules and algorithms: pricing, parsing, permissions, state machines.
- **Integration tests** run several real parts together, typically your code plus a real database or HTTP layer. They catch what unit tests structurally cannot: wrong SQL, missing migrations, serialization mismatches, middleware order.
- **Contract tests** check that a consumer and a provider agree on an interface (Pact is the best-known tool) without deploying both. They replace a lot of slow cross-service end-to-end tests.
- **End-to-end (E2E) tests** drive the real app through a browser or API as a user would. Few, slow, and valuable for the handful of journeys that must never break (sign up, checkout).
- **Regression tests** are any test added because a bug happened. Write the failing test first, then fix: the bug can never silently return.
- **Smoke tests** are a tiny post-deploy check that the service is alive and the main path works.

The classic picture is a **pyramid** (many unit, fewer integration, few E2E). The **testing trophy** popularized in the frontend world argues for a fatter middle: mostly integration tests that render a component with its real children and assert on what a user sees, because they are tied less tightly to implementation. Both agree on the principle: test behavior, push checks to the cheapest level that can catch them, and keep slow tests few.

### Anatomy of a good test

**Arrange, act, assert.** Set up the world, do one thing, check one outcome. A test with five unrelated assertions fails in confusing ways. Name tests as sentences describing behavior (`rejects_expired_coupon`), not methods (`test_apply`). Keep tests **independent** (any order, any subset, in parallel) and **deterministic** (same result every run).

**Test doubles** replace collaborators you do not want in a test. Be precise, because the words get mixed up:

| Double | What it does |
|---|---|
| Dummy | Fills a parameter; never actually used |
| Stub | Returns canned answers so the code under test can proceed |
| Fake | A real but simplified implementation, such as an in-memory repository |
| Spy | Wraps the real thing and records how it was called |
| Mock | Pre-programmed with expectations about calls, and fails if they are not met |

Prefer **fakes and real components over mocks** where practical. Heavy mocking ties tests to *how* the code works instead of *what* it does, so harmless refactors break dozens of tests, and the mocks drift from reality (the mock says the API returns a list; the real API returns a page object). Mock at the boundary you do not own (a payment provider, the clock, email), not between your own classes.

### Tools you will meet

- **Python: pytest.** Plain `assert`, fixtures for setup and teardown, `@pytest.mark.parametrize` to run one test over many inputs, `tmp_path`, `monkeypatch`, and a huge plugin ecosystem (`pytest-asyncio`, `pytest-cov`, `pytest-xdist` for parallel runs). The 9.x line was current in the sources I checked.
- **JavaScript and TypeScript: Vitest or Jest.** Vitest reuses your Vite config, runs TypeScript natively and has a Jest-compatible API, and was in its 4.1.x releases as of mid to late 2026. Jest remains common in older and React Native codebases. For HTTP handlers, Supertest drives an Express app without opening a port.
- **Browser: Playwright.** Drives Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, with auto-waiting actions, role-based locators (`getByRole`), a trace viewer for debugging CI failures, and an agent-assisted workflow for planning and generating tests that arrived in 1.56. Cypress is the other widely used option.
- **Real dependencies: Testcontainers.** Starts a throwaway Postgres or Redis in Docker for the test run, so integration tests use the real engine rather than SQLite pretending to be Postgres.
- **Beyond examples: property-based testing** (Hypothesis for Python, fast-check for TypeScript) states a rule ("decoding an encoded value returns the original") and lets the tool generate hundreds of inputs, then shrinks a failure to a minimal example. **Mutation testing** (mutmut, Stryker) deliberately breaks your code and checks that some test fails, which measures whether tests actually assert anything.

### Coverage is a flashlight, not a score

Code coverage tells you which lines ran, not whether anything checked them. A test that calls a function and asserts nothing gives 100% coverage and zero protection. Use coverage to **find untested areas**, set a floor to stop it silently dropping, and be suspicious of any target treated as the goal. Branch coverage is more honest than line coverage; mutation score is more honest still.

### Determinism: the cure for flaky tests

A **flaky test** passes and fails on the same code. It trains the team to ignore red builds, which is how real failures ship. Nearly all flakiness comes from a short list: real time (`sleep`, "today"), randomness without a seed, test order dependence and shared state, network calls, concurrency races, and UI waits on fixed delays. Fixes: inject the clock and random source, seed randomness and log the seed, give each test its own data and cleanup, wait for conditions rather than durations, and never call the real internet. Quarantine a flaky test immediately (tracked, with an owner and a deadline) rather than retrying until green.

### TDD and where it helps

Test-driven development is a loop: write a failing test, write the least code to pass, refactor with the test as a safety net. It shines for well-specified logic and bug fixes, and it shapes designs to be testable (small functions, injected dependencies). It is a tool, not a religion: for exploratory UI or a spike you do not yet understand, write tests after the shape settles.

## Worked example

A checkout discount rule, tested at three levels. The business rules: 10% off orders of 100 or more, free shipping at 50 or more after discount, and a coupon can only be used once per customer.

```python
# pricing.py
from dataclasses import dataclass
from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP

CENT = Decimal("0.01")

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Quote:
    subtotal: Decimal
    discount: Decimal
    shipping: Decimal
    total: Decimal

def quote(subtotal: Decimal) -> Quote:
    if subtotal < 0:
        raise ValueError("subtotal must be non-negative")
    discount = (subtotal * Decimal("0.10")).quantize(CENT, ROUND_HALF_UP) if subtotal >= 100 else Decimal("0.00")
    after = subtotal - discount
    shipping = Decimal("0.00") if after >= 50 else Decimal("4.99")
    return Quote(subtotal, discount, shipping, (after + shipping).quantize(CENT, ROUND_HALF_UP))
```

**Unit tests** with parametrization, including the boundaries where bugs hide (99.99, 100.00) and a property:

```python
# test_pricing.py
from decimal import Decimal
import pytest
from hypothesis import given, strategies as st
from pricing import quote

@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "subtotal, discount, shipping, total",
    [
        ("0.00",   "0.00",  "4.99", "4.99"),    # empty-ish basket pays shipping
        ("49.99",  "0.00",  "4.99", "54.98"),
        ("50.00",  "0.00",  "0.00", "50.00"),   # boundary: free shipping starts at 50
        ("99.99",  "0.00",  "0.00", "99.99"),   # boundary: no discount yet
        ("100.00", "10.00", "0.00", "90.00"),   # boundary: discount starts at 100
    ],
)
def test_quote_rules(subtotal, discount, shipping, total):
    q = quote(Decimal(subtotal))
    assert (q.discount, q.shipping, q.total) == (Decimal(discount), Decimal(shipping), Decimal(total))

def test_rejects_negative_subtotal():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        quote(Decimal("-1"))

@given(st.decimals(min_value=0, max_value=100_000, places=2))
def test_total_is_never_negative_and_never_exceeds_subtotal_plus_shipping(subtotal):
    q = quote(subtotal)
    assert q.total >= 0
    assert q.total <= subtotal + Decimal("4.99")
```

**An integration test with a fake** for the once-per-customer coupon rule. The service takes a repository; the fake is a dictionary in memory, so the test needs no database but still exercises the real service logic:

```python
class FakeCouponRepo:
    def __init__(self): self.used = set()
    def has_used(self, customer, code): return (customer, code) in self.used
    def mark_used(self, customer, code): self.used.add((customer, code))

def test_coupon_can_only_be_used_once_per_customer():
    svc = CouponService(FakeCouponRepo())
    assert svc.redeem("cust-1", "WELCOME") is True
    assert svc.redeem("cust-1", "WELCOME") is False   # second use rejected
    assert svc.redeem("cust-2", "WELCOME") is True    # other customers unaffected
```

Add one more integration test against a **real Postgres via Testcontainers** that runs the real migration and proves the `UNIQUE (customer_id, code)` constraint holds under two concurrent redemptions. That is the test the fake cannot give you, and it is exactly the race a mock would hide.

**An E2E test** for the single journey that matters, in Playwright with TypeScript. It uses roles and visible text, not CSS selectors, and no fixed sleeps:

```ts
import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test("a customer can check out with a discounted basket", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("/shop");
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Add to basket" }).first().click();
  await page.getByRole("link", { name: "Basket" }).click();
  await page.getByLabel("Quantity").fill("10");
  await expect(page.getByText("Discount")).toBeVisible();   // auto-waits and retries
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Pay now" }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole("heading", { name: "Order confirmed" })).toBeVisible();
});
```

For time-dependent frontend code in Vitest, fake the clock instead of waiting:

```ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi, afterEach } from "vitest";
import { isExpired } from "./coupon";

afterEach(() => vi.useRealTimers());

describe("isExpired", () => {
  it("is true one second after the expiry", () => {
    vi.useFakeTimers();
    vi.setSystemTime(new Date("2026-10-17T12:00:01Z"));
    expect(isExpired(new Date("2026-10-17T12:00:00Z"))).toBe(true);
  });
});
```

## In real products

- **Google** has described a testing mix of roughly 70% small, 20% medium and 10% large tests in its public writing, and invests heavily in hermetic (self-contained) tests and in tracking and fixing flakiness at scale.
- **Stripe, Shopify and Netflix** are among companies that publish about contract testing, consumer-driven tests and testing in production (canaries, feature flags, shadow traffic) as complements to pre-merge tests.
- **Most CI systems** (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI) split slow suites across parallel runners (sharding) and cache dependencies, because suite speed is a team-wide tax paid on every push.
- **Open-source libraries** such as pytest, Vitest and Playwright test themselves across many operating systems and language versions in CI, which is why their releases are trustworthy enough to build on.
- **LLM applications** need a different layer: datasets of inputs, graders and regression gates for non-deterministic output. That is covered in the evals lesson; the discipline (small fast checks first, a few expensive ones last) is the same.

> [!pitfall] Testing implementation instead of behavior: asserting that a private method was called twice, or snapshotting a whole rendered tree. The first refactor breaks everything and teaches the team to delete tests. Assert on outputs and observable effects.
> [!pitfall] Over-mocking. When every collaborator is a mock, the test mostly verifies your mock setup, passes while production is broken, and fails on harmless refactors. Use fakes or real components for your own code and mock only true external boundaries.
> [!pitfall] Treating coverage as the target. Coverage rewards calling code, not checking it, and chasing 100% produces assertion-free tests. Use it to find holes and add mutation testing on the code that matters most.
> [!pitfall] Sharing state between tests (a global, a reused database row, a leftover file). Tests pass in one order and fail in another, and parallel runs become impossible. Give each test its own data and clean up in fixtures.
> [!pitfall] Retrying flaky tests until they go green. It hides the bug (often a real race in production code) and slows every build. Quarantine, find the cause, and fix or delete.
> [!security] Never put real secrets or production data in test fixtures or CI logs. Use generated fake data, scoped test credentials, and an isolated test environment; a leaked fixture is a leak. Tests are also a good place to encode security rules: assert that user A cannot read user B's object.
> [!prod] Run the fast suite on every commit and the slow one on merge or nightly, fail the build on any red, and track the flaky-test rate like an SLO. A suite people trust gets run; a suite people distrust gets bypassed with the skip flag.
> [!cost] Slow tests cost real money (CI minutes) and more in developer waiting time. Measure the slowest tests regularly, parallelize, avoid unnecessary full-database resets, and move checks down the pyramid where they are cheaper.
> [!tip] When you find a bug, write the failing test before the fix. It proves you reproduced the right bug, it documents the case forever, and it is the cheapest regression test you will ever write.
q: Why is 100% code coverage not proof that the code is well tested?

Coverage only shows which lines ran. A test that calls a function and asserts nothing still counts. Use coverage to find untested areas and mutation testing to check that tests actually assert behavior.
What is the difference between a stub, a fake and a mock?

A stub returns canned answers, a fake is a simplified working implementation (such as an in-memory repository), and a mock has expectations about how it will be called and fails if they are not met. Prefer fakes over mocks for your own code.
Name four common causes of flaky tests and a fix for each.

Real time (inject a clock or use fake timers), unseeded randomness (seed and log the seed), shared state or test order (isolate data per test), fixed sleeps in UI tests (wait for a condition). Network calls are another: replace them with fakes.
When would you choose an integration test with a real database over a unit test with a fake?

When the behavior depends on the database itself: SQL correctness, migrations, constraints and concurrency. A fake cannot reveal that a unique constraint is missing or that two concurrent writes race.
What does property-based testing add over example-based tests?
You state a rule that must hold for all inputs, and the tool generates many cases, including odd edge cases you would not write, then shrinks a failure to a minimal example.
Why write the failing test before fixing a bug?
It proves you reproduced the real bug, then confirms the fix, and leaves a permanent regression test so the bug cannot silently return.
